questions.question: Which statement best captures bilinearity for a pairing e: G1 × G2 → GT?
options: e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)^(ab) for scalars a, b and points P, Q
e(P + Q, R) = e(P, R) + e(Q, R) in the target group GT
e(P, Q) = e(Q, P) for all points P, Q (symmetry is required)
e(P, Q) is a hash of (P, Q) that looks random but is reproducible
questions.explanation: Bilinearity means linear in each argument, which gives e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)^(ab) in the multiplicative target group.

questions.question: In a reduced Tate pairing, what is the main purpose of the final exponentiation step?
options: Force the output into the subgroup of r-th roots of unity so the pairing is well-defined
Convert an elliptic curve point into a compressed SEC1 public key encoding
Make scalar multiplication constant-time by removing secret-dependent branches
Guarantee that every input point is on the curve without doing validation
questions.explanation: The final exponentiation maps a Miller function value into μ_r ⊂ F_{p^k}^*, removing ambiguity from multiplying by r-th powers.

questions.question: What does it mean for a point P to be in the r-torsion group E[r]?
options: r·P = 𝓐 (the point at infinity)
P has x-coordinate less than r
P is defined over the base field F_p (not an extension field)
P generates the entire elliptic curve group E(F_p)
questions.explanation: E[r] is the set of points killed by multiplication by r, i.e., points with r·P = 𝓐.

questions.question: What kind of objects does the Miller loop repeatedly evaluate at a point Q?
options: Line functions from the elliptic-curve group law (tangents/secants and related denominators)
Discrete logarithms of Q with respect to a generator of G2
Hashes of intermediate points to randomize the computation
Square roots in F_p to lift x-coordinates back to points
questions.explanation: Miller’s algorithm multiplies together evaluations of rational functions built from the same lines used in point addition and doubling.

questions.question: Why do pairing constructions typically work over an extension field F_{p^k} rather than just F_p?
options: Because the r-th roots of unity μ_r and enough r-torsion points may only exist over F_{p^k}
Because elliptic curves cannot be defined over prime fields
Because point addition is undefined over F_p but works over F_{p^k}
Because extension fields automatically make operations constant-time
questions.explanation: The target group GT is a subgroup of F_{p^k}^*, and the full E[r] structure often only appears over a suitable extension field.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what is the core idea behind the MOV reduction on weak parameters?
options: Use a pairing to map an elliptic-curve discrete log instance into a finite-field discrete log instance
Use a pairing to turn ECDSA signatures into plaintext messages
Use a pairing to compute square roots mod p faster than exponentiation
Use a pairing to bypass point-on-curve checks during key parsing
questions.explanation: When the embedding degree is small, pairings can reduce ECDLP in an r-torsion subgroup to DLP in a subgroup of F_{p^k}^*.

questions.question: Which identity reflects the alternating property of the Weil pairing?
options: e(P, P) = 1 for all P in E[r]
e(P, Q) = e(Q, P) for all P, Q in E[r]
e(P, Q) = 0 whenever P and Q are nonzero points
e(P, Q) always equals 1 whenever P and Q are in the same subgroup
questions.explanation: An alternating pairing satisfies e(P, P) = 1, which is one reason you need two “independent” r-torsion points for nontrivial values.

questions.question: For a reduced Tate pairing on F_{p^k}, which exponent is applied after the Miller function evaluation?
options: p^k − r
questions.explanation: The reduced Tate pairing raises the Miller function output to (p^k − 1)/r to land in μ_r.
